feature: Does the app need project types?
summary: A study, not a build. It answers the question you raised about project types: yes the app should ask what you are making, no it should not use the answer to hide anything. The New sheet is drawn, the editor is drawn twice under two different kinds with everything the kind removes still visible, and the document that breaks the idea is drawn beside them.
setup: A browser at http://127.0.0.1:8791/index.html#project-kinds (Icons ▸ "Does the app need project types?"). Nothing in the app changed, so there is nothing to launch. A decision card is waiting on the dashboard.

try.do: Open the study page and read the first paragraph, which is the whole answer in six lines.
Look at the New sheet in section 1. This is the half of the idea the study says to keep.
Scroll to section 2 and compare the two editors. Red slashes mark what each kind has taken away.
Read the last row of the table under them: five slots gone for an icon, zero for a capture.
Scroll to section 4 and look at the 24 point bell beside the 1440 screen. That document is legal in Photonz today.
Scroll to section 5 and compare the two windows there: same document, no kind, every tool present, different panel.
Open the decision card on the dashboard and pick an option.

evaluate: Does the New sheet in section 1 look like something you would want, separately from the hiding question?
Is the icon-beside-its-screen document in section 4 a thing you would actually make, or is it an argument invented to win?
In section 2, does the icon window read as focused or as broken?
Section 5 changes the panel without asking a question. Is that enough relief, or does the toolbar still need to get shorter?
The recommendation leaves the toolbar carrying all thirteen tools forever. Is that acceptable?
rough: No app change was made, so there was no walk to run and no window to photograph. The three pictures are of the study page itself in a browser, which is the deliverable here.

The honest gain from hiding is larger than the study's conclusion makes it sound: five of thirteen tool slots for an icon and seven for a recording. If you weigh a quiet window higher than a tool never going missing, option b is a defensible choice and the study would be wrong.

Section 5 leans on a rule with a hole in it: a picture opened from a file has no frame around it, so a capture document has nothing for the context to follow. That is named in the recommendation as slice 2 rather than solved.

The Recording column of the tool census describes a window that does not exist yet in the layer document. It is drawn as if video had moved in, because that is the only way to compare it, and that is a guess about a surface nobody has built.

The study did not test the recommendation against a person who has never used the app. It argues from what the app already does, which is strong evidence about correctness and weak evidence about whether the four starting points are the right four.
